    AI Overview
    Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic, often disabling autoimmune disease where the immune system attacks the protective myelin sheath covering nerve fibers in the brain and spinal cord. It causes communication issues between the brain and body, leading to symptoms like vision loss, pain, fatigue, and impaired coordination. While there is no cure, treatments can manage symptoms and slow progression. 
    Early Signs and Symptoms
    MS symptoms are often unpredictable and vary widely depending on the location of the nerves affected, appearing commonly between ages 20 and 40. 
    • Vision Problems: Blurred/double vision or pain with eye movement (optic neuritis).
    • Sensory Changes:
      Numbness, tingling ("pins and needles"), or burning sensations, often in limbs or face.
    • Weakness/Balance Issues: Muscle weakness, fatigue, or difficulty with coordination and balance.
    • Other Early Signs: Vertigo, bladder dysfunction, and cognitive fatigue. 
    Causes and Risk Factors
    The exact cause of MS is unknown, but it is considered an autoimmune disease. 
    • Immune System Dysfunction: The immune system mistakenly attacks myelin and nerve fibers, causing inflammation and scarring (lesions).
    • Risk Factors:
      • Age: Typically diagnosed between 20 and 40, though it can affect children and older adults.
      • Gender: Women are nearly three times more likely to develop MS than men.
      • Genetics: A parent or sibling with MS increases risk.
      • Environment: Higher prevalence in temperate climates. 
    Prognosis and Daily Life 
    • Prognosis: While there is no cure, most people with MS have a near-normal life expectancy, with many remaining active and mobile for years, particularly with modern treatments.
    • Daily Life: Management requires a team approach, including disease-modifying therapies, medication, and physical therapy to treat flare-ups. Disease courses vary, with most experiencing relapsing-remitting MS (periods of attacks and recovery) or progressive forms (gradual worsening). 
    Types of Multiple Sclerosis 
    • Relapsing-remitting MS (RRMS): Most common (85%), featuring temporary flare-ups (relapses) followed by remission.
    • Secondary progressive MS (SPMS): Follows RRMS, with a gradual worsening of neurological function.
    • Primary progressive MS (PPMS): Less common, defined by slowly worsening symptoms from the start without relapses.
    • Progressive-relapsing MS (PRMS): Rare; steady decline with occasional acute relapses. 
    Disclaimer: This information is for informational purposes only and does not constitute medical advice. Consult a healthcare provider for diagnosis and treatment.
